_comment: Permissions for the Claude Skills Toolkit (github.com/LunarCommand/claude-skills).
Merge into ~/.claude/settings.json. The toolkit installs as one plugin at user scope,
so its permissions belong at the same scope; a per-project copy means re-approving the
same toolkit in every repository. That is safe only because this file covers this
toolkit and nothing else. Without it, every bundled script prompts on each call, which
reads as the skill being broken.
Nothing applies this for you — plugin.json has no permissions field and a plugin
cannot ship a settings layer. lunar_install.sh merges it on request: it reports by
default and writes only under --apply, and it prompts every call because a rule
approving it would sit in the file it writes.
Scripts are approved by BARE NAME, never by path: bin/ reaches the Bash tool's PATH
through the plugin. A bare name failing with 'command not found' means the plugin is
not loaded, not that the rule is wrong.
The ask list is deliberate, and deliberately broader than the allow list's rule of
tracing to a command a shipped skill runs. An ask rule grants nothing: listing one costs
a prompt, and leaving one out costs nothing right up until a broad allow rule or auto
mode would have let the command through unasked, which is the moment it was for. So it
covers the class rather than the subset these skills happen to call: what
install/user/CLAUDE.md says never to do without an ack (commit, push, amend, rebase,
force-anything, touching files outside the plan), what its Releases section says to
confirm before (tag, publish), and the tree- or history-mutating git commands
adversarial-review's own instructions forbid. Those are prose in a skill and a prompt
here, which is the difference between an instruction an agent should follow and one it
cannot quietly skip. git submodule foreach is here because the snapshot genuinely runs
it and it takes an arbitrary command string. rm and git worktree remove are here on a
different footing: a rule matches what the agent types into the Bash tool, not what an
approved script runs inside itself, so the six rm calls and the worktree teardown these
scripts make are untouched by either rule. No SKILL.md asks the agent to run either one
-- the worktree runner even hands its own teardown command to you under --keep -- so
the rules cost the toolkit nothing and cover what adversarial-review's Step 0 exists to
prevent. git worktree prune is listed for the reason the runner gives for not calling
it: prune is repo-wide and would deregister an unrelated worktree of yours whose
directory is merely unavailable.
curl and wget are a deliberate trade. The hyperdx and langfuse skills forbid reaching
past their scripts for data and state that doing so prompts, which is only true while
something here makes it true. The cost is a prompt on langfuse SKILL.md's documented
fallback for fetching public docs -- a path that same section already tells the agent
to prefer WebFetch over.
The deny list is the environment, and only the environment. These scripts take their
API keys from it: .agent.env is loaded into the script's own process, but an exported
LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY works too, so env or printenv prints a live key into the transcript,
and a transcript is not somewhere a key can be withdrawn from. Denying export also makes
langfuse SKILL.md's 'never export env vars manually' something an agent cannot skip.
env, set and export -p are matched EXACTLY, not as prefixes -- do not 'fix' them to :*.
The README's 'What a permission rule actually matches' is the one place the rule
semantics these files depend on are written down; read it before changing a rule.
What is deliberately NOT denied here: credential directories and shell histories.
Denying a path at user scope asserts a filesystem policy over every repository you open,
and no shipped skill traces to one -- that belongs in your own settings, or in
install/project/settings.json, which carries ~/.ssh and two cloud config directories as
examples.
Everything else from one ~/.claude/settings.json -- attribution, notifications, effort
-- sits in settings.optional.json beside this file, which carries no permissions key so
this stays the only file here that grants anything.
EDIT THIS FILE AS TEXT. Do not round-trip it through a JSON serialiser to add a rule:
the blank lines inside these arrays group them into blocks a reader navigates by, and
they are whitespace a serialiser drops. One such pass re-sorted the allow list, flattened
every group in ask, and escaped the em-dashes above. The JSON is identical and the file
is no longer readable, which is the whole value of a list this long.
